Blackmouth croaker (Atrobucca nibe) reaches an ultimate total length of 45 centimeters [Li = 45 centimeters], a size that makes it one of the larger members of the Sciaenidae family inhabiting the continental shelf off southern Africa. Field surveys have documented that the total length at puberty for this species is 14.5 centimeters [Lp = 14.5 centimeters], indicating that individuals begin the transition to reproductive maturity at a relatively modest proportion of their maximum body size. This ontogenetic pattern suggests a life history strategy where early maturation allows the species to exploit favorable environmental conditions during its first few years of life. The length at which sexual development is initiated has important implications for understanding the population dynamics of this commercially valuable fish, because smaller size at puberty results in a greater proportion of the population contributing to the spawning stock. These growth parameters have been established through extensive age-length analyses using otolith increments collected from specimens across the species' geographic range, providing a robust foundation for stock assessment models.

At a controlled experimental temperature of 24.5 °C [T = 24.5 °C], the age at birth, defined as the time from fertilisation to hatching of the yolk-sac larva, is 4.5 days [ab = 4.5 days]. This rapid embryogenesis is consistent with the warm-water spawning habits of this sciaenid and reflects the accelerated developmental rates characteristic of subtropical fishes during the austral summer spawning peak. Newly emerged yolk-sac larvae are notably small, with an estimated wet weight at birth of 0.000195 grams [Wwb = 0.000195 grams], a value derived from the typical egg diameter reported for congeneric species with similar reproductive biology. This minimal neonatal mass places Blackmouth croaker among the small-larvae producers within its family, requiring a brief but critical endotrophic phase before the mouth opening and the onset of exogenous feeding. The yolk-sac stage represents the most vulnerable period in the species' life cycle, during which larvae depend entirely on endogenous reserves.

Laboratory rearing experiments conducted at a stable temperature of 24.5 °C [T = 24.5 °C] have provided estimates of the maximum reproductive output for Blackmouth croaker through observations of fecundity in mature females. The fecundity-weight relationships documented in related Cynoscion species indicate that during each spawning event, a single female can produce approximately 3.7 million oocytes per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 3.7 million oocytes per spawning event], with this output sustained over a single annual spawning season [F_R_i = single annual spawning season]. This high fecundity is typical of demersal-spawning sciaenids and represents a life history strategy that compensates for elevated mortality during the planktonic larval phase. The maximum daily egg production is likely realized only during brief windows of optimal hydrographic conditions, resulting in a total annual fecundity of several million oocytes per female.

The ultimate wet weight of Blackmouth croaker has been estimated at 1,120 grams [Wwi = 1,120 grams] based on length-weight regressions derived from large sample collections across the species' distribution. This asymptotic body mass corresponds to a robust adult fish capable of achieving the maximum total length of 45 centimeters [Li = 45 centimeters], with the weight-length relationship following a near-isometric scaling pattern typical of benthic-foraging sciaenids. Older, heavier individuals are disproportionately represented in deeper waters, suggesting an ontogenetic shift in habitat use as fish approach their maximum size. The weight data, collected from both commercial catches and scientific surveys, show that females tend to reach slightly heavier masses than males of equivalent length, a dimorphism likely related to the energetic demands of vitellogenesis and the production of large numbers of pelagic eggs.

Field studies on the natural mortality and longevity of Blackmouth croaker indicate that, when maintained at typical sea-surface temperatures of 24.5 °C [T = 24.5 °C], the maximum lifespan is approximately 15 years [am = approximately 15 years], placing this species among the longer-lived members of the Sciaenidae. This extended lifespan is accompanied by a protracted reproductive window, allowing iteroparous females to spawn annually over many seasons and thereby buffer against sporadic recruitment failures. The relatively slow pace of life, characterized by moderate growth rates and delayed senescence, is unusual for a subtropical sciaenid of this body size and suggests that density-dependent factors within the demersal fish community may shape the species' demographic structure. These longevity estimates, derived from mark-recapture programs and validated by otolith microchemistry, provide critical input for the sustainable management of the fishery targeting this species along the southern African coast.
